uncited: Exponential decay schedules reduce the learning rate multiplicatively over training steps, providing a smooth, continuous transition from high initial exploration to fine-grained convergence.

This family differs from [Linear Learning Rate Schedule](11850-linear-learning-rate-schedule.md) by applying relative reductions rather than absolute ones, and from [Cosine Decay Learning Rate Schedule](14118-cosine-decay-learning-rate-schedule.md) by avoiding the symmetric "slow-fast-slow" trajectory in favor of a monotonic decrease .
It is primarily used in NeRF optimization to stabilize training when the model has converged to a coarse geometry but requires precise refinement of appearance and density fields.
All methods in this family compute the learning rate $lr_t$ at step $t$ using a base raised to a power proportional to the normalized step count.
where $\gamma$ is the decay factor ($0 < \gamma < 1$) and $T$ is a normalization constant (often total steps or a specific interval).
This ensures the learning rate never reaches zero but asymptotically approaches it.
Unlike step decay, there are no discrete jumps.
The schedule is often combined with warm-up phases to prevent early instability .
Exponential decay is a standard technique in optimization, widely adopted in early neural network training and retained in NeRF pipelines for its simplicity and effectiveness in fine-tuning .

In the context of differentiable volume rendering, it addresses the problem of converging sparse input data by preventing large gradient updates once the model has established a coherent geometric prior .
